title_patterns: [SPECIFIC DOLLAR FIGURE] of insider buying across [N] stocks — one outlier stands out
[TICKER] just filed a [specific transaction type] most investors missed
[NAMED EXPERT/INSTITUTION] says [specific mechanism] is finally repricing — here's the data
Earnings breakdown: [TICKER] [quarter] numbers vs. what was priced in
[N] stocks trading below [specific valuation metric] after the drawdown
What actually moved the [specific market/asset class] this week — in [N] charts
[Policy/Treasury action] explained: what it changes for [specific yield/sector] math
Why [sector] companies are buying back stock at [specific pace/number]
hook_patterns: Open with one unrounded figure from a filing or print, then state what it does and does not tell you
Name the single question the video answers, then show the data source on screen before any commentary
Lead with a named expert's specific claim, then immediately test it against the actual series
State the consensus expectation, then the reported number, then the gap — in the first 20 seconds
Start with 'here's what changed in the data since last week,' followed by a bounded list of items
packaging_notes: Two duration clusters appear: 6–12 minute single-topic explainers (earnings reactions, one insider move, one policy action) and 19–29 minute multi-holding or multi-stock roundups. Pick one lane per video rather than splitting.

Titles carrying a specific dollar amount or a stock count (e.g. '$500M+', '8 stocks', '5 stocks') recur across the set; unrounded, verifiable numbers are the on-brand version of this and avoid hype framing.

Named-source framing ('says [expert]', '[official]'s move') travels well in this niche — attribution does the curiosity work without needing alarm language, and is reusable for a numbers-first channel.

Earnings-event packaging appears twice for the same ticker on the same day, suggesting event-windowed uploads matter more than title novelty; publishing inside a few hours of the print is the structural lever.
Several outliers here are political-outrage or drama-driven and are not transferable to this positioning — treat their view counts as audience-specific, not as evidence that escalation framing works.
Views-per-hour, not total views, separates this-week momentum from long-tail accumulation; the highest VPH items are event-tied, which argues for a fast-turnaround data recap format.
market_patterns.title: outlier pattern extraction

winning_patterns.pattern: Two-clause title where the second clause corrects the obvious interpretation (an 'X — but the real driver is Y' / 'A, not B' reframe)
winning_patterns.evidence: Our two highest-retaining non-contrast Shorts both used a corrective second clause and landed at 76.0% and 68.9% APV with hook hold above 1.07 — above the 65.0% cohort average.
winning_patterns.why_it_may_work: The title states a fact and then pre-commits to an explanation the viewer can't derive themselves, so the payoff is inside the video rather than in the headline.
winning_patterns.how_to_reuse: Keep the structure: [ticker + verified move] + [short clause that rules out the intuitive cause]. Cap the second clause at ~4 words.

winning_patterns.pattern: Single-name event paired with a volatility reading rather than an index level
winning_patterns.evidence: Three Shorts that paired a stock-specific event with a VIX move retained 71.9%, 68.3% and 89.2%; the two that paired a stock move with a Dow or Nasdaq move retained 55.9% and 53.7%.
winning_patterns.why_it_may_work: A volatility number implies a regime the single name is fighting, which sets up a question; a broad index number reads as boilerplate context.
winning_patterns.how_to_reuse: When adding market context to a single-ticker title, prefer the volatility stat if it is genuinely relevant. Treat this as a correlation on 5 videos, not a rule.

winning_patterns.pattern: Headline number plus a flagged mechanical cause (corporate action, timing, structural quirk)
winning_patterns.evidence: The Short that attached a huge percentage move to a mechanical trigger held 84.9% APV despite being one of our lowest-view videos (50).
winning_patterns.why_it_may_work: It signals the video explains why a number is misleading, which fits a data-first audience that expects the catch.
winning_patterns.how_to_reuse: Where a move is driven by a split, reclassification, listing mechanic or timing artifact, name that mechanic in the title instead of amplifying the percentage.

winning_patterns.pattern: Named-person franchises (congress_trade, insider_watch) hold mid-to-high and convert engagement best
winning_patterns.evidence: Both named-person Shorts posted 68.9% and 68.3% APV with hook hold above 1.06, and the highest engaged-view shares in the set (roughly 46% and 43% of views vs a ~38% cohort level).
winning_patterns.why_it_may_work: A named actor plus a dollar or position size gives the hook a subject, not just a delta.
winning_patterns.how_to_reuse: Keep [named person] + [size of the action] + [one-clause reframe] as the standing shape for these two franchises.

losing_patterns.pattern: Bare 'percent move + benchmark move' titles with no explanatory clause
losing_patterns.evidence: The three Shorts that were only a move plus context and no 'why' hook sat at the bottom of retention: 55.9%, 53.7% and 50.3% APV, all with hook hold below 0.93.
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: The title delivers the whole datapoint, so the first seconds have nothing left to promise.
losing_patterns.fix: Always reserve one clause for the mechanism, the contradiction or the unresolved question.

losing_patterns.pattern: Procedural or timestamp detail used as the hook (legal-process framing, clock times)
losing_patterns.evidence: Our weakest-retaining Short led with a move and then a procedural timestamp; 50.3% APV, hook hold 0.868 — last in the cohort.
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: Process minutiae signals a narrow administrative story rather than a market consequence.
losing_patterns.fix: Convert procedural detail into consequence framing (what it changes for the tape) or leave it in the body.

losing_patterns.pattern: Titles that state the outcome and then resolve the tension themselves
losing_patterns.evidence: The Short whose second clause reassured that the situation continues had the worst hook hold in the set (0.778) and 58.2% APV.
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: Answering your own setup in the title removes the reason to stay past the first seconds.
losing_patterns.fix: End the title on the open half of the tension, not the resolution.

losing_patterns.pattern: Static level or status titles (closing price, first-day-of-something) without a delta or conflict
losing_patterns.evidence: A price-level Short landed mid-pack at 58.3% APV and our lowest view count in that group (57), underperforming every title with a reframe clause.
losing_patterns.why_it_hurts: A level alone carries no direction and no stake for the viewer.
losing_patterns.fix: Pair any level with what it contradicts or what it implies next.

notes: All 11 videos are Shorts, so there is no long-form read in this window and no duration comparison should be inferred. Views are low (48-181), so every pattern here is directional at best.

market_close carries most of our volume and has the widest retention spread (50.3%-84.9%); the split tracks title structure — cause/reframe clause versus bare move — more than the size of the move itself. A 1,400% move and a -44.7% move sat at opposite ends of retention.

Views and retention are decoupled: our highest-view Short (181) ranked 4th in APV, while two of the three best-retaining Shorts had under 80 views. hook_hold and avg_view_pct move together almost mechanically here, so treat them as one signal, not two independent confirmations, and do not read APV as evidence of feed conversion.
own_patterns.title: own-channel lessons
